feedback: If the net closes with no gaps or overlaps you have a valid cube net; if two faces collide or a gap remains, the arrangement cannot be a cube even though it has six squares
When you predicted the opposite face, check after folding: opposite faces never share an edge in the flat net
If a pupil counts 'six squares' and stops, prompt them to fold the look-alike and name exactly which two faces collide

Note that the real paper or card net has a slight thickness and is a close stand-in for the ideal zero-thickness mathematical surface; the reasoning is about the mathematical shape it folds into, not the card itself
activities.intendedInsight: Having six squares is not enough — the arrangement must actually fold into a closed solid. Folding real nets makes the fold relationships concrete before pupils are asked to imagine them.
learnerActions: Cut out and fold a real cube net from paper or card and check it closes with no gaps or overlaps
Fold a look-alike net that has the same six squares but in which two faces overlap or leave a gap, and observe that it refuses to close
Before folding each net, choose a base face and say aloud which face you think will land opposite it, then fold to check
Build a cube-shaped solid and a triangular prism from interlocking construction pieces (e.g. polydron), joining flat faces until the solid closes
activities.title: Fold real nets by hand: valid vs look-alike

feedback: If a pupil fails to name a tilted cuboid, ask them to describe the faces they can see and reason about the hidden ones (a cuboid has six rectangular faces in matching opposite pairs) rather than expecting the standard view
Turning a solid does not change what it is — if it has six square faces it is still a cube on whichever face it rests
Linking net <-> solid <-> isometric in both directions checks the connection is understood, not just memorised one way
activities.intendedInsight: A shape is defined by its faces and properties, so it stays the same shape in any orientation and across net, solid and isometric representations.
learnerActions: Name the 3-D shape shown in isometric drawings of the same solid in several different orientations, including non-standard ones (e.g. a cuboid drawn at an angle or resting on an unfamiliar face)
Justify each name by its faces/properties rather than by matching a single prototypical picture
Go both directions: predict the solid from a given net, and sketch or point to a valid net for a given solid
Optionally use a wrap/unwrap view — fold a net onto a rotatable solid and turn the solid to confirm it is the same shape whichever face it rests on, keeping a flat-net view alongside
activities.title: Recognise solids in any orientation and link representations
